subject: psychology
topic: Knowing the truth about a topic can actually make you believe it less
angle: Meta-analyses of fear appeals and climate change consensus messages show positive effects on attitudes and behaviors without evidence of backfiring.
title: The mechanics of belief

hooks.text: Does knowing the truth make you believe it less?
You think fear makes people shut down. The evidence says otherwise.
You choose to ignore the warnings that actually work.
A red light flickers in a dark hallway.

reveal.headline: Fear appeals do not backfire.
reveal.body: Research shows no identified circumstances where fear leads to undesirable outcomes.

explain.headline: Information shapes your behavior.
explain.body: Fear appeals have a positive effect on your attitudes and actions. Consensus messages on climate change also show small but significant positive effects regardless of your politics.

matters.headline: The truth is not a wall.
matters.body: That may be why you feel more capable of change when faced with facts. You might still feel a sense of resistance, but the evidence suggests the facts are moving you forward.

example.headline: A warning on a screen.
example.body: You see a headline about a rising tide or a looming threat. You feel a pulse in your throat. You read the data. You decide what to do next.

question.headline: What are you waiting to hear?

stat.label: average effect of fear appeals on attitudes, intentions, and behaviors

claims.text: There are no identified circumstances under which fear appeals backfire and lead to undesirable outcomes.
claims.quote: Overall, we conclude that (a) fear appeals are effective at positively influencing attitude, intentions, and behaviors; (b) there are very few circumstances under which they are not effective; and (c) there are no identified circumstances under which they backfire and lead to undesirable outcomes.

claims.text: Fear appeals have a positive effect on attitudes, intentions, and behaviors, with an average effect on a composite index of random-effects d = 0.29.
claims.quote: Results showed a positive effect of fear appeals on attitudes, intentions, and behaviors, with the average effect on a composite index being random-effects d = 0. 29.

claims.text: The effect of consensus messages on climate change attitudes was small yet statistically significant and positive (g = 0.09), and was not significantly moderated by political affiliation.
claims.quote: The effect of consensus messages on attitudes was small yet statistically significant and positive (g = 0.09), and not significantly moderated by political affiliation.

claims.text: There is little meta-analytic evidence that consensus messages backfire.
claims.quote: While conservatives may experience resistance to consensus messages, there is little meta-analytic evidence that consensus messages backfire.

verdict: The evidence suggests that providing facts or using fear appeals generally leads to positive outcomes rather than reinforcing original misconceptions.
caveat: The study on climate change consensus messages specifically notes that while there is no evidence of backfiring, some individuals may still experience psychological reactance.
caption:
You may believe that facts only cause people to dig in their heels.

Meta-analyses show that fear appeals and consensus messages generally lead to positive changes in behavior and attitude. Some individuals may still experience psychological reactance, but the data does not show evidence of backfiring.

How does your perspective shift when the facts are clear?
